(1) domain swapping in OBPb is controlled by a glycine residue in the hinge linking beta-barrel to alpha-helix, and by the presence at the dimer interface of the C-terminus and of the lipocalin conserved disulfide bridge.

the dimeric form of bovine odorant binding protein (OBP) can be transformed into the monomeric form by mutating the residue 121, and that the dimerization of OBPb is controlled by the C- terminus, by a glycine in position 121, by a disulphide bond between cysteines 114 and 144 and by a beta-turn between residues 121 and 126.
the domain swapping of OBPb is controlled by two factors, one structural and the other sequence-related.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and functional analysis of proteins involved in the olfaction.
the structural and functional characterization of bovine and pig odorant binding proteins, which are two of the most abundant proteins in the mammalian nasal epithelium.
the structural and functional characterization of the domain swapping process, and with the role of the conserved disulphilde bridge in the dimerization process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
domain swapping is a reversible process, which can be controlled by a few amino acid substitutions.
OBPb is a domain swapped lipocalin dimer, whereas OBPp is a monomeric lipocalin.
the domain swapping in OBPb is controlled by the combination of two features, the absence of the glycine 121 and the presence of the disulphide bond.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of the conserved cysteine residue and the presence of a Gly in the hinge region of the beta-turn are both required for dimerization, and that a Gly is not enough to reverse the dimerization.

the domain-swapped dimer of OBPb is a rare case of an oligomerization mode for a lipocalin, and that domain swapping is not an evolutionary pathway to oligomerization, but rather a mechanism for the formation of dimers in lipocalin family proteins.
domain swapping is controlled by a combination of factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
domain swapping can be easily reversed by a single mutation, and that domain swapping is not a necessary step for lipocalin oligomerization.
domain swapping in OBPs is a reversible process.
domain swapping can be controlled in the lipocalin fold, and this may be a common mechanism for controlling the oligomeric state of proteins.
